procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated November 24, 1964 of the Assam and Nagaland High Court in Civil Rule No. 208 of 1964.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Assam and Nagaland passed a judgment and order in Civil Rule No. 208 of 1964 under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. The High Court quashed the order of the Board of Revenue.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's decision. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the order of the High Court, and restored the order of the Board of Revenue.

directions: The order of the High Court is set aside and that of the Board of Revenue is restored.
The respondent will pay the costs of the appellant.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in holding that the effect of compounding an offence under Section 62 of the Assam Forest Regulation was the same as an acquittal under Section 345(6) of the Criminal Procedure Code, and that consequently, no moral turpitude was involved which could affect a person's suitability for the settlement of an excise shop.

facts: The respondent, a forest contractor, had previously compounded an offence under the Assam Forest Regulation for illegally felling green trees by paying compensation.
When the respondent was granted the settlement of an excise shop, the Board of Revenue overturned it, deeming him unsuitable due to this prior conduct.

The High Court reversed the Board's decision, ruling that compounding the forest offence was equivalent to an acquittal under Section 345(6) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.), and therefore, no moral turpitude could be attached to the respondent's character.
law: Section 345(6) of the Cr.P.C. explicitly states that the composition of an offence *under that section* shall have the effect of an acquittal. This effect is limited to the specific offences listed within Section 345.

Section 62 of the Assam Forest Regulation empowers a forest officer to accept compensation from a person *suspected* of committing a forest offence to avoid prosecution. This section does not contain any provision stating that this action has the effect of an acquittal.
The Court noted that unless a law expressly provides that compounding an offence amounts to an acquittal, the mere act of paying compensation does not vindicate the character of the person charged.
application: The Supreme Court distinguished between the two laws. It held that the principle of acquittal under Section 345(6) Cr.P.C. could not be extended to the Assam Forest Regulation because the Regulation lacked a similar express provision.

The Court reasoned that a person might pay compensation under the Forest Regulation simply to avoid the harassment of a prosecution, not because they are innocent. This act does not remove the suspicion against them.

The Court viewed the respondent's payment of compensation as an "acceptance of the charge against him." It concluded that this action did not clear his character and only protected him from further legal proceedings for that specific offence.

Therefore, the conduct did involve moral turpitude, and the Board of Revenue was justified in considering it when assessing the respondent's suitability and moral character for the settlement of an excise shop.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's reasoning. It held that compounding an offence under Section 62 of the Assam Forest Regulation does not have the effect of an acquittal, unlike offences compounded under Section 345 of the Cr.P.C. Consequently, the Board of Revenue was correct in considering the respondent's conduct, which involved moral turpitude, when determining his suitability for the settlement of an excise shop.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Board of Revenue exceeded its jurisdiction or committed an error apparent on the face of the record by taking into consideration the compounded forest offence when assessing a candidate's suitability.

facts: The Board of Revenue rejected a candidate's (Hazarika's) application for an excise shop license, deeming him unsuitable.

The Board's decision was based on the fact that the candidate had previously, as a forest contractor, illegally felled green trees and compounded the offence by paying compensation under the Assam Forest Regulation.

The High Court quashed the Board's order, reasoning that compounding the offence had the effect of an acquittal (based on an analogy with the Criminal Procedure Code), and therefore the Board could not consider the incident.
law: The Court distinguished between compounding an offence under the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) and under the Assam Forest Regulation.
Under Section 345(6) of the Cr.P.C., compounding an offence is explicitly stated to have the effect of an acquittal.

However, Section 62 of the Assam Forest Regulation, which allows for compounding, does not state that it amounts to an acquittal. It only protects the person from further proceedings for that specific offence.
The authority granting an excise shop license is entitled to consider the 'conduct' and 'moral character' of a candidate to determine their suitability.
application: The Supreme Court ruled that the High Court was wrong to equate compounding under the Forest Regulation with an acquittal under the Cr.P.C.
Because compounding the forest offence did not amount to an acquittal, it did not erase the underlying conduct or vindicate the candidate's character.
The Board of Revenue was assessing the candidate's overall suitability, a process in which considering past conduct is a valid and relevant factor.

Therefore, the Board was well within its jurisdiction to take into account the fact that the candidate had illegally felled trees, even if the offence was later compounded. This act was relevant to his character and suitability for the license.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Board of Revenue did not exceed its jurisdiction or commit an error of law. The Board was entitled to consider the conduct that led to the compounded forest offence as a relevant factor in assessing the candidate's suitability. Consequently, the High Court was not justified in quashing the Board's order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the appellate order of the Board of Revenue by issuing a writ of certiorari under Article 226 of the Constitution.

facts: The Board of Revenue, in an appeal concerning the settlement of an excise shop, held that the respondent was not a suitable person for the license.
The Board's decision was based on the fact that the respondent, a forest contractor, had previously compounded an offence of illegally felling trees by paying compensation.
The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court, which quashed the Board's order.
The High Court reasoned that compounding the offence had the effect of an acquittal, and therefore the Board was not entitled to take that conduct into account when assessing suitability.
law: The jurisdiction of a High Court to issue a writ of certiorari under Article 226 is limited.
A writ of certiorari can be issued if an inferior tribunal acts in excess of its jurisdiction or commits an error of law apparent on the face of the record.
Certiorari is not meant to take the place of an appeal and cannot be used to correct every error of law or fact.
The powers of an appellate authority, like the Board of Revenue, in matters of settlement are co-extensive with the powers of the primary authority.
application: The Supreme Court found that the Board of Revenue was competent and had not exceeded its jurisdiction when it took the respondent's past conduct into consideration.
The Board was entitled to take the view that the respondent's act of compounding a forest offence reflected on his suitability and vigilance in observing the law.

The Supreme Court held that the High Court was incorrect in its legal conclusion that compounding an offence under the Assam Forest Regulation was equivalent to an acquittal under the Criminal Procedure Code.
Since the Board of Revenue had not exceeded its jurisdiction or committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record, there was no basis for the High Court to interfere.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in quashing the appellate order of the Board of Revenue. The Board had acted within its legal authority by considering the respondent's conduct, and the High Court overstepped the limited scope of its certiorari jurisdiction by interfering with that decision.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in holding that the effect of compounding an offence under Section 62 of the Assam Forest Regulation was the same as an acquittal under Section 345(6) of the Criminal Procedure Code, and that consequently, no moral turpitude was involved which could affect a person's suitability for the settlement of an excise shop.
appellant_arguments: Section 345(6) of the Criminal Procedure Code does not apply to an offence compounded under the Assam Forest Regulation.
respondent_arguments: The principle behind compounding an offence under Section 62 of the Assam Forest Regulation is the same as an acquittal under Section 345(6) of the Criminal Procedure Code.
The forest offence in question was a very minor one, and compounding it by paying compensation should not impute any stigma on the character of the person involved.
The legislative intent for allowing compounding of trivial offences is that they should not be brought up again or taken notice of in the future.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Board of Revenue exceeded its jurisdiction or committed an error apparent on the face of the record by taking into consideration the compounded forest offence when assessing a candidate's suitability.
appellant_arguments: The Board of Revenue acted within its jurisdiction by considering the compounded forest offence as a relevant factor for assessing a candidate's suitability, as such compounding is not equivalent to an acquittal that erases the conduct.
respondent_arguments: The Board of Revenue exceeded its jurisdiction by considering an irrelevant and impermissible factor, as compounded trivial offences should not be raked up again or taken notice of.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the appellate order of the Board of Revenue by issuing a writ of certiorari under Article 226 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The High Court was not justified in interfering with the Board of Revenue's order, as the Board had not acted in excess of its authority or committed an error of law.
respondent_arguments: The High Court was justified in exercising its controlling authority because the Board of Revenue acted in excess of its legal power by considering the compounded offence.

cases.case_name: Nagendra Nath Bora & Anr. v. The Commissioner of Hills Division and Appeals, Assam & Ors.
cases.principle: The jurisdiction of the High Court to issue a writ of certiorari is invoked for an error of law apparent on the face of the record, not every error of law or fact. A writ of certiorari is not an appeal; its purpose is to determine if an inferior tribunal exceeded its jurisdiction or failed to follow the essential requirements of the law it administers.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An appellate authority, in determining questions affecting the right to the settlement of a liquor shop, does not exceed its jurisdiction or commit an error of law apparent on the face of the record by taking into consideration a candidate's past conduct, such as the rendering of compensation for a forest offence. Consequently, the High Court is not justified in quashing such an order through a writ of certiorari.
obiter: The jurisdiction of the High Court on certiorari may be invoked for an error of law apparent on the face of the record, and not for every error of law or fact which can be corrected by a superior court in its capacity as a court of appeal or revision.

An order of certiorari is not meant to take the place of an appeal; its purpose is only to determine whether the inferior tribunal had exceeded its jurisdiction or had not proceeded in accordance with the essential requirements of the law.
The powers of the Appellate Authorities in the matter of settlement are co-extensive with the powers of the primary authority.

If a person is charged with an offence, then unless there is some provision for composition of it, the law must take its course and the charge enquired into, resulting either in conviction or acquittal.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's central finding is that compounding an offence under Section 62 of the Assam Forest Regulation is not equivalent to an acquittal. The court reasoned that the payment of compensation under the Regulation amounts to an "acceptance of the truth of the charge" against the person. While this action protects the individual from further proceedings for that specific offence, it does not have the effect of clearing their character or vindicating their conduct. Therefore, the compounded offence was a relevant factor for the Board of Revenue to consider when assessing a candidate's suitability, and doing so was not an error of law.
legal_tests_applied: The jurisdiction of a High Court to issue a writ of certiorari may be invoked for an error of law apparent on the face of the record, not every error of law or fact. A writ of certiorari is not meant to take the place of an appeal; its purpose is to determine whether the inferior tribunal exceeded its jurisdiction or failed to proceed in accordance with the essential requirements of the law.
policy_considerations: While the law allows for the composition of certain offences to provide procedural finality, this does not erase the underlying conduct itself. An agreement to compound an offence does not mean the conduct is ignored for all future purposes, especially when an administrative body is assessing a person's character for a public privilege.
